children: Norse Atlantic Airways, which had won over some thrifty travelers despite charging for blankets and earphones on its flights, suspended operations Thursday and stranded hundreds of holiday travelers in the U.S., the U.K. and elsewhere as it made a last-ditch push to avoid bankruptcy.

The discount airline's Thanksgiving Day cancellations included flights between Orlando and London. The company's already stretched finances have been pressured by rising fuel costs this year, with the airline saying a day earlier that its financial position was critical.

Norse Atlantic said Thursday it was ceasing flying operations to focus on a final effort with investors to secure short-term funding or a possible takeover that would give it enough cash to continue flying, though it said it wasn't sure any deal would be reached.

"Under the circumstances the company has suspended all of today's flights," Norse said. "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy."

A small airline, with just 12 aircraft in its fleet, Norse Atlantic had won over loyalty among passengers for pricing that often far undercut rivals like British Airways. But it also burned through cash and accumulated losses.

The upstart's move to halt flying comes two days after it launched its "Black Flyday" Thanksgiving sale, offering 10% off flights to destinations including Orlando, Phuket and Cape Town. Tickets for flights in the coming months were still available to book on its website as of early Thursday.

It is the latest in a string of airlines that have been pushed to the brink by the surge in oil prices since the U.S. and Israel started their campaign against Iran in late February. The Islamic Republic's response in the war has upended shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and destroyed refineries used to produce jet fuel.

The sudden and sustained hike in prices precipitated the collapse of Spirit Airlines in May, pushed Europe's AirBaltic into filing for Chapter 11 protection in September, and has left JetBlue Airways fighting to stem investor concerns about the airline's ability to survive a prolonged crisis.

Norse itself was born of a 2021 bankruptcy, picking up the Boeing 787 fleet and long-haul, low-cost ambitions abandoned by its forebear, Norwegian Air Shuttle, during the latter's pandemic-era bankruptcy proceedings.

Some of Norse's biggest investors previously led Norwegian's ambitious expansion to overseas markets, including former chief executive Bjorn Kjos and chairman Bjorn Kise. The new airline's impending collapse would mark the end of their second attempt to revolutionize long-haul travel for passengers by stripping out bells and whistles — in Norse's case, that included asking travelers to fork out $7 for blankets and $5 for plug-in earphones.
